title: India's Central Bank Just Made Dollar Deposits Ridiculously Attractive for NRIs. Here's the Math.
excerpt: The RBI is absorbing all hedging costs on foreign currency deposits, banks are offering 6–7% yields, and with leverage, wealthy NRIs can earn up to 22% annualised returns on a fixed-income product. The window closes September 30.
body:
India's Reserve Bank of India has pulled a move straight from the 2013 playbook — but this time, the numbers are even more dramatic.

Earlier this month, the RBI announced it would absorb the full hedging cost on foreign currency non-resident deposits — known as FCNR(B) deposits — for terms of three to five years. The scheme is designed to pull dollar flows from the 37-million-strong Indian diaspora and shore up a rupee that had been battered to record lows during the US-Iran war.

But what started as a currency defence measure has quietly become one of the most attractive dollar-denominated investment opportunities NRIs have seen in years.

## What Changed

Under normal circumstances, Indian banks offering FCNR(B) deposits must hedge against currency risk, which eats into the returns they can offer. The cost of that hedge — typically 2–3 percentage points — made these deposits uncompetitive with US Treasuries.

The RBI's new scheme eliminates that drag entirely. With hedging costs at zero, banks can now offer rates of **6% to 7%** on dollar deposits, well above the 4.2% yield on three-year US Treasury notes. The scheme runs until September 30, with a swap facility available through October 16.

State Bank of India, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Bank of Baroda and other major lenders have already begun marketing the deposits aggressively in the US, UK, Canada and the Gulf — the largest Indian diaspora corridors.

## The Leverage Play



> **"The scheme is designed to pull dollar flows from the 37-million-strong Indian diaspora and shore up a rupee that had been battered to record lows during the US-Iran war."**


The real excitement, though, is around leverage.

The RBI has explicitly allowed Indian banks to issue standby letters of credit against FCNR(B) deposits, enabling depositors to borrow against their own holdings and reinvest the proceeds into fresh deposits. In effect, a depositor can multiply their position several times over.

According to Emkay Global Financial Services, an NRI investor putting in $1 million and leveraging it nine times — building a $10 million deposit — could earn annualised returns of roughly **21.8%** on their original capital. Even at more conservative leverage of three to five times, returns work out to 11.6% and 15% respectively.

"For NRIs, this is a very good product because they are getting 6% yield and they can typically borrow eight to nine times in their respective markets at 4–4.5%," said Rohan Mandora, a research analyst at Equirus Securities.

## The Catch

Financial advisers are quick to add caveats. The leveraged play is structured for ultra-high-net-worth individuals, not retail depositors. The overseas loans that fund the leverage are typically floating-rate, meaning a rise in global borrowing costs can erode returns quickly across a leveraged position. Processing fees, standby letter of credit costs (0.5–1% annually) and documentation charges further compress the spread.

Rahul Agarwal, a SEBI-registered investment adviser, told Mint he is actively advising clients *against* leveraging. "The deposit pays a fixed rate, but the overseas loan funding is usually on a floating rate, so even a small rise in global borrowing costs can significantly erode returns because the investor is leveraged multiple times over," he said.

For most NRIs, the straightforward unleveraged play — parking disposable savings in a 6–7% dollar deposit for three to five years, with no currency risk — is itself a compelling proposition.

## How Much Will Flow In

Estimates range from bullish to very bullish. Nomura pegs potential inflows at **$55 billion**, with the bulk expected in August and September. Axis Bank sees scope for as much as $100 billion. Punjab National Bank expects to raise $2.5–3 billion on its own.

The scheme has already begun producing side effects in India's banking system. Bulk domestic deposit rates fell 40–50 basis points after the announcement, as banks shifted their funding strategy toward cheaper FCNR inflows.

## What NRIs Need to Know

The deposits are available in any freely convertible currency, though the RBI's swap facility applies only to US dollars. There is a one-year lock-in period on the underlying deposit. Principal and interest are fully repatriable on maturity, and the product eliminates exchange-rate risk — the RBI bears it.

For NRIs earning in dollars and looking for a safe, high-yield parking spot for three to five years, this is arguably the best deal India has offered since the Raghuram Rajan-era FCNR window of 2013. That scheme pulled in $34 billion and was widely credited with stabilising the rupee during the taper tantrum.

This time, the scale could be larger. The question is whether the rupee — currently around 94.68 per dollar — can absorb the eventual unwinding when these deposits mature and the dollars flow back out.

## The Diaspora Angle

India has a long history of turning to its diaspora in moments of currency stress. The Resurgent India Bonds of 1998, the India Millennium Deposits of 2000 and the FCNR(B) scheme of 2013 were all crisis-era instruments that doubled as expressions of diaspora loyalty.

This scheme is different in one respect: it is pitched not as patriotic duty but as pure financial logic. The economics genuinely favour the depositor — at least for now.
